<reason>A established a coherent distinction between revisable multiyear commitments and aid requiring repeated renewal. It directly addressed oversight, conditionality, and emergency weapons reallocation while accepting genuine resource sacrifices. B identified important opportunity costs, but repeatedly treated a standing commitment as necessarily irrevocable or meaningless rather than defeating A's intermediate model. A's planning, production, and Russian-waiting mechanisms consequently survived. Its cost-benefit comparison remained qualitative, but B did not establish why additional withdrawal flexibility outweighed those benefits.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's distinction between democratic reversibility and routine expiration defeated B's central binding-or-meaningless dilemma. A also correctly rejected B's claimed falsification: the absence of a decisive Russian breakthrough does not disprove an argument that uncertain aid increases vulnerability and rewards waiting.</best_rebuttal>
